prequestions.prompt: Before money existed, early societies ran their economies on barter.

prequestions.prompt: In the UK, roughly what share of the money people hold is notes and coins?

sections.title: A fortune at the bottom of the sea
sections.intro_md:
On Yap, a small island group in the western Pacific, one family was counted among the richest on the island even though nobody alive had ever seen their fortune. It was a huge limestone disc that had fallen off a raft during a storm and sunk to the seabed generations earlier. Everyone agreed the stone still existed and still belonged to them. So it still worked as wealth.

That story, written down by the American anthropologist **William Furness** in **1910**, is the best short answer to today's question. Money is not the stone, the coin or the note. Money is a shared record of who owes what to whom, plus enough trust that the record will be honoured tomorrow.

Today you will test that idea against 5,000 years of evidence: clay tablets, cowrie shells, Lydian coins, Chinese paper, notched sticks that burned down Parliament, Indian rupees, hyperinflation, UPI and Bitcoin. By the end, the ₹500 note in your wallet should look a lot stranger than it does now.

spotlights.name: Rai stones of Yap
spotlights.when: Quarried over several centuries; still exchanged in ceremonies today
spotlights.spot_it: Giant stone wheels with a hole in the middle, leaning against walls and palm trunks along village paths.
spotlights.story_md: Yapese sailors quarried the limestone on **Palau**, about **400 km** away, and brought the discs home by canoe and raft. The biggest surviving stone, on **Rumung**, is **3.6 metres** across and weighs about **4 tonnes**. Value came from size, craft and history: a stone that cost lives to bring home was worth more. Big stones almost never moved. When one changed hands, the island simply remembered the new owner. In the 1870s an Irish-American captain, **David O'Keefe**, began shipping stones with iron tools and a schooner. Yapese valued his easy stones lower than the hard-won old ones, which is a monetary policy in miniature.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Rai show money working as a public ledger, with no need for the token to move.
spotlights.memory_hook: On Yap you can be rich in a stone you have never seen.

spotlights.name: Milton Friedman's 'Island of Stone Money'

where.label: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

spotlights.spot_it: The Nobel economist in big glasses who used Yap to explain a 1930s gold panic.
spotlights.story_md: In **1991** Milton Friedman wrote a short essay pairing Yap with Paris. In **1932** the Banque de France, fearing the dollar would be devalued, asked the Federal Reserve Bank of New York to turn its dollar balances into gold. The gold never crossed the Atlantic. Fed staff moved bars into compartments in the New York vault and labelled them as French property. Newspapers reported a 'loss of gold' by the United States, which fed the banking panic of early **1933**. Friedman's point: the French felt richer and the Americans felt poorer because of marks on drawers in a basement, just as Yapese counted a stone on the seabed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that even 'hard' gold money runs on records and belief.
spotlights.memory_hook: Gold that moved one drawer to the left helped start a bank panic.

sections.title: Three jobs, one promise
sections.intro_md:
Economists define money by what it does, not what it is made of. It has three jobs. It is a **medium of exchange** (you hand it over and walk off with the goods). It is a **unit of account** (prices, salaries and debts are written in it). And it is a **store of value** (it still buys something next month). A fourth job, a **standard of deferred payment**, lets you sign a loan today in a unit both sides will recognise in ten years.

Anything that does those jobs well enough is money: shells, salt, cigarettes, entries in a bank's computer. Anything that stops doing them, like the Zimbabwe dollar in 2008, stops being money even if it is still printed.

The numbers below show how far modern money has drifted from metal. Most of it is not cash. In the United Kingdom, **97%** of the money people hold is bank deposits, not notes and coins. In India, notes worth about **₹40 lakh crore** circulate, and UPI moved more than **24 billion** payments in a single month of 2026.

spotlights.name: Aristotle on money
spotlights.spot_it: Marble bust of a bearded Greek philosopher; the idea is in Book V of the Ethics.
spotlights.story_md: Aristotle saw something that later economists keep rediscovering. The Greek word for coin, **nomisma**, comes from **nomos**, meaning law or custom. In the Nicomachean Ethics he argued that money exists not by nature but by convention, and that it is in our power to change it or make it useless. He also described its job as a common measure that makes unlike things, a house and a pair of shoes, comparable. In the same breath he called charging interest the most unnatural way to make money, a view that shaped Christian and Islamic rules on usury for 2,000 years.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first serious thinker to say money is a social agreement, not a thing.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nomisma comes from nomos: coin comes from custom.

spotlights.name: Reserve Bank of India
spotlights.spot_it: Solid stone RBI offices like the Kolkata and Nagpur buildings; the emblem is a tiger and a palm tree; headquarters on Mint Road, Mumbai.
spotlights.story_md: The RBI was set up on **1 April 1935** under the RBI Act of 1934 and nationalised in **1949**. It is the sole issuer of banknotes in India, with one quirk: the **₹1 note** is issued by the Government of India and signed by the finance secretary, not the RBI governor. Coins are minted by the government too. The RBI decides how much cash to print, sets the repo rate that steers bank lending, and keeps the country's reserves, including **880.52 tonnes** of gold at the end of March 2026. Every note above ₹1 carries the governor's signature under the line 'I promise to pay the bearer the sum of...', a promise that today means only another note.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the institution behind the trust in every rupee you hold.
spotlights.memory_hook: The ₹1 note is the government's; every other note is the RBI's promise.

sections.title: The barter story that never happened
sections.intro_md:
Every economics textbook tells the same origin myth. Before money, people bartered. The baker wanted meat, the butcher wanted shoes, and trade stalled because wants rarely matched. So people settled on one commodity everyone accepted, and that became money.

It is a tidy story, popularised by **Adam Smith** in **1776**. The problem is evidence. Anthropologists have searched for a society that ran on barter and never found one. Caroline Humphrey of Cambridge concluded in **1985** that no barter economy has ever been described, let alone one that turned into a money economy.

What the record shows instead is **credit**. In villages, people tracked who owed whom and settled up later, often never. In Mesopotamia, temple and palace scribes kept accounts in barley and silver on clay tablets about **5,000 years** ago, long before coins. Barter does happen, but mostly between strangers, or after money collapses: in Russia in the 1990s, in prisoner-of-war camps, in Argentina in 2001. The order was credit first, coins later, barter as a fallback.

spotlights.name: Adam Smith and the double coincidence of wants
spotlights.spot_it: Profile portrait of a Scottish philosopher in a wig; the passage is Book I, Chapter 4.
spotlights.story_md: Smith imagined a butcher with more meat than he needs and a brewer and baker who want some but have nothing he wants in return. Money, he argued, was invented to solve that mismatch, which later economists called the **double coincidence of wants**. Smith even offered a live example: a village in Scotland where, he had heard, workmen carried **nails** to the baker's shop instead of money. Later historians pointed out that the nails were almost certainly credit: the nail-makers were paid in nails by their employers and the baker kept a running tab. Smith's story was a thought experiment that hardened into history.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most repeated origin story in economics rests on almost no observation.
spotlights.memory_hook: Smith's nails were an IOU dressed up as barter.

spotlights.name: The anthropologists' verdict
spotlights.spot_it: Field reports from Himalayan villages to Pacific islands, none showing a barter economy.
spotlights.story_md: Caroline Humphrey studied trade in Nepal and elsewhere and published her review, 'Barter and Economic Disintegration', in **1985**. Her finding, repeated by David Graeber and many others: barter appears between people who do not trust each other or will never meet again, not inside a community. Neighbours do not swap a cow for six shirts. They give, help, borrow and remember, and the obligation sits in social memory. Economists such as George Selgin push back that early credit still needed something like a unit of account, which is fair. But on the narrow claim that whole economies once ran on barter, the evidence is close to zero.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The textbook story is a hypothesis that failed its field test.
spotlights.memory_hook: Neighbours keep tabs; only strangers swap cows.

spotlights.name: Clay ration tablets of Mesopotamia
spotlights.spot_it: Palm-sized clay tablets with round dents for numbers and tiny pictures of heads, bowls and barley.
spotlights.story_md: Some of the oldest writing on Earth is not poetry or law. It is accounting. Tablets from Uruk and Jemdet Nasr in what is now Iraq record rations of barley and beer issued to workers, using a picture of a head next to a bowl for 'ration'. One famous tablet, often called the **Kushim tablet**, records **29,086** measures of barley over 37 months, as usually read, and carries what may be the first personal name ever written. Debts were recorded in barley and silver long before anyone stamped a coin. Writing and money grew up together as tools for remembering obligations.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Money as a unit of account came thousands of years before coins.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first written name may belong to an accountant.

spotlights.name: Interest caps in the Code of Hammurabi

where.label: Louvre Museum, Paris (found at Susa, Iran)

spotlights.spot_it: A black basalt pillar over two metres tall, a king facing a seated god at the top, dense cuneiform below. Louvre, Paris.
spotlights.story_md: King Hammurabi of Babylon had nearly 300 laws carved on this stele, and several deal with debt. They set the maximum interest a lender could charge: about **20% a year on silver** and about **33% on barley**, reflecting how risky a harvest loan was. One law said that if a storm destroyed a farmer's crop, his debt payments that year were washed away too. The **shekel**, which survives as Israel's currency, started as a weight of barley and silver, about 8 grams. Mesopotamian kings also proclaimed periodic debt cancellations, wiping out farmers' consumer debts to stop them falling into bondage.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Credit, interest and debt relief were regulated 1,200 years before coins.
spotlights.memory_hook: Babylon capped interest at 20% before anyone had a coin.

spotlights.name: David Graeber and 'Debt: The First 5,000 Years'
spotlights.spot_it: A rumpled American anthropologist at a microphone; also known for the phrase 'We are the 99%'.
spotlights.story_md: Graeber, an anthropologist at the London School of Economics, published **Debt: The First 5,000 Years** in **2011**, the year he helped shape the Occupy Wall Street movement. His argument: credit and debt came first, coins came with armies and empires, and history swings between eras of virtual credit money and eras of hard metal. He pointed out that words for debt and sin overlap in many languages. Economists criticised parts of the book, especially its broad historical claims, but it moved the barter myth out of footnotes and into public debate. Graeber died in Venice on **2 September 2020**, aged 59.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made 'credit came first' a mainstream idea outside anthropology.
spotlights.memory_hook: Debt is older than coins, and Graeber made millions read about it.

sections.title: Shells, salt, copper and cigarettes
sections.intro_md:
Before and alongside coins, people used useful or beautiful objects as money. Economists call this **commodity money**: the token has value as a thing as well as a means of payment.

Good commodity money shares a few traits. It is **durable** (shells do not rot), **portable**, **divisible** into small amounts, **hard to fake**, and **limited in supply**. Cowries scored well on all five, which is why they served as money across Africa, South Asia and China for about **3,000 years**.

Commodity money has a weakness: its supply depends on nature or industry, not on what an economy needs. When European ships brought tonnes of Maldivian cowries to West Africa in the 1800s, the shells lost value fast. When a prison camp's supply of cigarettes dried up, prices collapsed. The same problem, too much or too little of the money stuff, returns in every later section.

spotlights.name: Cowrie shells
spotlights.when: From about 1500 BCE in China; into the 1900s in Africa and India
spotlights.spot_it: Small, glossy, egg-shaped shells with a toothed slit on the underside.
spotlights.story_md: The money cowrie, **Monetaria moneta**, lives in the shallow lagoons of the **Maldives**, which harvested and exported them for centuries. Shang dynasty tombs in China are full of them, and the Chinese character for valuables, 貝, began as a picture of a cowrie; it still sits inside the characters for buy, sell and treasure. In India, cowries made up the smallest change, and the phrase **'phooti kaudi'** (a broken cowrie) still means worthless. In West Africa, merchants shipped billions of shells from the Maldives via Bengal and later Zanzibar, and by the late 1800s inflation had made them almost useless.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The longest-running and most widespread currency in human history.
spotlights.memory_hook: A broken cowrie still means worthless in Hindi.

spotlights.name: Manillas of West Africa
spotlights.spot_it: Open horseshoe-shaped bracelets of brass or copper with flared ends.
spotlights.story_md: Portuguese traders arriving on the West African coast in the 1400s found that copper was prized, so they shipped brass rings made in Europe. These **manillas** became money in the Niger Delta, and they were used to pay for enslaved people in the Atlantic trade. Bronze plaques from the Kingdom of Benin show Portuguese men holding manillas. They stayed legal currency in British Nigeria until the colonial government ran **Operation Manilla** in **1948 to 1949**, buying in more than **32 million** of them for the new West African pound and selling them as scrap metal.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A trade good that turned into money, and a reminder of what that money bought.
spotlights.memory_hook: Brass bracelets were legal tender in Nigeria until 1949.

spotlights.name: Tea bricks
spotlights.when: Tang dynasty onward; used as money into the 20th century
spotlights.spot_it: Dark, pressed slabs of tea leaves, often stamped with characters and scored into squares.
spotlights.story_md: Tea leaves pressed into hard bricks travelled well along the tea-horse routes from China into **Tibet, Mongolia and Siberia**. Far from the tea gardens, a brick was worth more, so it worked as money: people priced horses, wool and salt in bricks and broke off pieces as change. It was the rare currency you could also drink. Travellers in Mongolia in the early 1900s reported paying in tea bricks for food and lodging, and a brick could be scored into squares like a chocolate bar for small purchases.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows how money's value depends on distance and scarcity.
spotlights.memory_hook: Small change you could boil and drink.

spotlights.name: Katanga crosses
spotlights.spot_it: X-shaped copper ingots, about the size of a hand, with a raised rib along each arm.
spotlights.story_md: Copper miners in what is now southern Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia poured molten copper into X-shaped sand moulds. The crosses served as currency and as a store of wealth for centuries, and were used to pay bride-price. Sizes were fairly standard, so they worked as units. A typical cross weighed about half a kilo. Some museum collections still hold the clay moulds used to cast them. A Katanga cross even appears on the flag of the short-lived State of Katanga in 1960.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A standardised metal ingot is one short step from a coin.
spotlights.memory_hook: Money cast in the shape of a cross from Congo's copper belt.

spotlights.name: Salt money and the 'salary' myth
spotlights.when: Ethiopian salt bars into the 20th century
spotlights.spot_it: Long grey slabs of rock salt, cut from the Danakil depression and carried by camel.
spotlights.story_md: Salt really was money in places. In Ethiopia, bars of rock salt called **amole** were cut in the **Danakil depression** and used as currency into the 20th century; their value rose the further they were carried from the salt flats. But the popular story that Roman soldiers were **paid in salt**, and that this is where 'salary' comes from, is shaky. The only ancient hint is a remark by **Pliny the Elder**. Historians find no evidence of salt wages, and the Latin **salarium** may have been an allowance for buying salt or something else entirely.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A good test case for separating real commodity money from a catchy myth.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ethiopia paid in salt; Rome probably did not.

spotlights.name: Cigarette money in a prisoner-of-war camp
spotlights.spot_it: Loose cigarettes from Red Cross parcels, traded by men in a Second World War prison camp.
spotlights.story_md: R. A. Radford, a British officer held in Italian and German camps, published 'The Economic Organisation of a P.O.W. Camp' in **1945**. With no cash, prisoners priced chocolate, jam and razor blades in **cigarettes**, even non-smokers. Prices rose and fell like a real economy. When Red Cross parcels arrived, cigarettes were plentiful and prices jumped; as stocks were smoked, deflation set in. Prisoners smoked the good machine-made cigarettes and spent the thin hand-rolled ones, a live example of Gresham's law: bad money drives out good. In US federal prisons after a **2004** smoking ban, inmates switched to pouches of **mackerel**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A clean natural experiment: money appears on its own wherever trade does.
spotlights.memory_hook: In the camp, the money supply went up in smoke.

sections.title: The coin: metal with a stamp
sections.intro_md:
A coin is a lump of metal with a promise stamped on it. The stamp says that someone powerful guarantees its weight and purity, so you do not need to weigh and test it every time. That saved enormous effort, and it let rulers pay soldiers in something the soldiers could spend anywhere.

Coins appeared in three places at roughly the same time, apparently independently: in **Lydia** in western Turkey, in the Ganges plain of **India**, and in **China**. Each took a different form. Lydians struck lumps of electrum with a lion. Indians punched symbols into cut silver. Chinese cast bronze in the shape of tools.

Once coins existed, a new temptation came with them. A ruler who controlled the mint could mix in cheaper metal and spend the difference. This is **debasement**, and Rome is the classic case. The profit a government makes by issuing money worth more than it costs to make is called **seigniorage**, and every central bank still earns it.

spotlights.name: Lydian electrum lion coins
spotlights.spot_it: Small, thick, irregular lumps of pale gold with a roaring lion's head on one side and punched squares on the other.
spotlights.story_md: The first coins in the Western record were struck in the kingdom of **Lydia**, around its capital **Sardis**, from **electrum**, a natural alloy of gold and silver washed down the river Pactolus. The earliest dated finds come from a foundation deposit at the **Temple of Artemis at Ephesus**, around 600 BCE. The problem with electrum is that its gold share varies from one deposit to the next, so a buyer could not judge a lump by eye. The king's stamp vouched for it. Greek writer **Herodotus** said the Lydians were the first people to use gold and silver coins and the first retail traders.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The coin, as a guaranteed token, begins here for the Mediterranean world.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first Western coins were lion-stamped lumps of river gold.

spotlights.name: Croeseid: the first pure gold coin
spotlights.spot_it: A bean-shaped gold coin showing a lion and a bull facing each other.
spotlights.story_md: Lydia's king **Croesus** solved electrum's problem by separating the metals. His mint refined gold and silver and struck coins of each, with a lion confronting a bull: the first **bimetallic** currency. Croesus became a byword for wealth, as in 'rich as Croesus'. His kingdom fell to Cyrus of Persia in **546 BCE**, and the Persians kept minting his design for years before replacing it with their own archer coins. Refining gold to a known purity is what made gold a trusted money for the next 2,500 years.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Pure, standard metal made coins comparable across borders.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rich as Croesus: he made the first pure gold coins.

spotlights.name: Athenian owl tetradrachm
spotlights.when: About 510 to 38 BCE; peak in the 5th century BCE
spotlights.spot_it: A thick silver coin with Athena's head on one side and a wide-eyed owl with an olive sprig on the other.
spotlights.story_md: Athens struck its owls from silver mined at **Laurion**, south of the city. A tetradrachm weighed about **17.2 grams** and was worth four drachmas, roughly four days' pay for a skilled worker in the 5th century BCE. Silver from Laurion paid for the fleet that beat Persia at Salamis in 480 BCE. The owls were trusted so widely that mints from Egypt to Bactria in Afghanistan copied them. They were the dollars of their age. Greece's modern **1 euro coin** carries the same owl.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first currency to work as an international reserve.
spotlights.memory_hook: Athens' owl flew from Egypt to Afghanistan and lands on Greek euros today.

spotlights.name: Chinese spade and knife money
spotlights.spot_it: Flat bronze shapes like little spades or knives, often with a hollow socket or a ring at one end.
spotlights.story_md: In China, coins began as models of tools. Farmers had once traded real bronze spades and knives, so states of the Zhou and Warring States periods cast miniature, unusable versions as money, marked with the issuing city's name. When the first emperor, **Qin Shi Huang**, unified China in **221 BCE**, he swept these away and imposed one coin: the round **ban liang** with a square hole, strung on cords in hundreds or thousands. The round-coin-with-square-hole design lasted for over 2,000 years, until the early 1900s.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Money's form copied the trade goods it replaced.
spotlights.memory_hook: Chinese money started as tools too small to dig with.

spotlights.name: Punch-marked coins of India
spotlights.spot_it: Small, flat, irregular silver pieces covered in punched symbols: suns, wheels, hills, animals.
spotlights.story_md: India's first coins were pieces of silver cut to a standard weight and stamped with several separate symbols using punches, rather than a single die. The standard unit, the **karshapana**, weighed about **3.4 grams** (32 ratis, a seed-based weight). They appear in the Mahajanapada kingdoms of the Ganges plain, such as **Magadha** and **Kosala**, from roughly the 6th or 5th century BCE, and the Mauryan empire issued them across the subcontinent. Grammarian **Panini** mentions coin terms, and the Arthashastra describes a mint superintendent. Most scholars see Indian coinage as an independent invention.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India was one of the three independent birthplaces of the coin.
spotlights.memory_hook: India's first rupees were silver stamped like a passport.

spotlights.name: The Roman denarius and its slow collapse
spotlights.spot_it: A small silver coin with an emperor's head; later versions look coppery and worn.
spotlights.story_md: Rome introduced the denarius around **211 BCE** at about 4.5 grams of nearly pure silver. Emperors short of cash for armies kept cutting its silver. Nero lowered it in 64 CE. By the reign of **Gallienus** in the 260s, the coin then in daily use, the antoninianus, held about **2% silver**, a copper coin with a silver wash. Prices soared. In **301 CE** Diocletian published an **Edict on Maximum Prices** fixing the cost of over a thousand goods; merchants hid stock and the edict failed. It is the oldest well-documented case of a government printing, or rather minting, its way into inflation.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first great lesson in what debasement does to prices.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rome's silver coin ended up 98% copper.

sections.title: Paper: money you cannot eat or melt
sections.intro_md:
Paper money is the moment money visibly becomes a promise. A note has almost no value as a thing. It works because people trust the issuer to accept it back, or to make others accept it.

China got there first, about **600 years** before Europe, and for a practical reason: Sichuan used heavy iron coins, and carrying a string of them to market was miserable. Merchants began issuing receipts; then the Song state took over. Within two centuries Chinese governments also discovered the dark side. Printing more notes was the easiest way to pay bills, and every dynasty that relied on paper eventually inflated it into worthlessness.

Europe's first banknotes came from Sweden in **1661**, for an equally physical reason: Swedish copper money came in plates weighing up to nearly 20 kg. India had its own paper instrument for centuries, the **hundi**, a merchant's bill that moved money across the subcontinent without moving a coin.

visual.title: Where money took its key forms

spotlights.name: Jiaozi: the world's first government paper money
spotlights.when: Private notes about 1000 CE; state issue 1023
spotlights.spot_it: A bronze printing plate showing houses, people and dense text, from Northern Song China.
spotlights.story_md: In Sichuan, iron coins were so heavy that a modest purchase meant hauling kilograms of metal. Around **1000 CE**, sixteen merchant houses in **Chengdu** issued paper receipts, called **jiaozi**, that could be swapped for coins. Some houses over-issued and failed, so in **1023** the Song government created an official bureau and took over. The notes were printed from plates in several colours with anti-forgery designs and had an expiry date, after which they had to be exchanged. By the 1100s the state was printing far more than it could back, and jiaozi lost most of their value.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Paper money began as a fix for heavy metal and a weak trust problem.
spotlights.memory_hook: China invented paper money because iron coins were too heavy.

spotlights.name: The Great Ming banknote
spotlights.spot_it: A large grey mulberry-paper note, about 34 by 22 cm, with a dragon border and strings of coins pictured in the centre.
spotlights.story_md: The **Da Ming Tongxing Baochao** is one of the largest banknotes ever issued, about the size of an A4 sheet. The founding Ming emperor issued it from **1375**, printed on mulberry bark paper, showing ten strings of coins to signal its value of one guan (1,000 copper cash). It carried a warning that counterfeiters would be beheaded and informers rewarded. The government issued notes without limit and never redeemed them, so they lost value quickly. By the mid-1400s the Ming had largely abandoned paper and turned to **silver**, much of which would later come from Spanish mines in the Americas.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A 600-year-old example of what unlimited printing does.
spotlights.memory_hook: The A4-sized note that promised death to forgers.

spotlights.name: Stockholms Banco: Europe's first banknotes
spotlights.spot_it: A handwritten-looking Swedish credit note from 1666 with several signatures and wax seals.
spotlights.story_md: Sweden's money in the 1600s included **copper plates**, the largest weighing nearly **20 kg**. **Johan Palmstruch**'s Stockholms Banco started issuing paper 'credit notes' in **1661** that people could carry instead. They were the first banknotes in Europe. The bank then issued more notes than it had copper to redeem, and by **1667** it collapsed. Palmstruch was sentenced to death, later commuted. Parliament replaced the bank in **1668** with the Riksens Ständers Bank, today the **Sveriges Riksbank**, the oldest central bank still operating. The Riksbank funds the economics prize awarded with the Nobels.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first European paper money also delivered Europe's first banknote crash.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sweden's money weighed 20 kg, so it invented paper.

spotlights.name: The hundi: India's merchant money
spotlights.spot_it: A narrow slip of paper in a merchant's script, with stamps and endorsements, sometimes several feet long when joined.
spotlights.story_md: Long before Indian banks issued notes, Indian merchant families, especially Marwari, Gujarati and Chettiar firms, moved money with the **hundi**, a written order to pay. A trader in Surat could hand cash to a shroff and receive a hundi payable by an associate in Benares, so no silver crossed bandit-filled roads. A **darshani** hundi was payable on sight; a **muddati** hundi after a set time. They could be endorsed and passed on, which made them circulate like money. The system ran on family reputation and was trusted by the Mughal state and the East India Company alike.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows that credit networks, not states, often created usable money.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hundi let a rupee travel without ever leaving Surat.

sections.title: Where most money really comes from
sections.intro_md:
Here is the fact that surprises most people. The bulk of the money in a modern economy is not printed by the government. It is created by **commercial banks** when they lend.

When a bank gives you a ₹10 lakh home loan, it does not take ₹10 lakh out of someone else's savings. It types ₹10 lakh into your account. That deposit is new money, matched by your debt to the bank. When you repay the loan, the money disappears again. The **Bank of England** spelled this out in a plain-English article in **March 2014**, adding that the old textbook 'money multiplier' gets the order wrong: loans create deposits, not the reverse.

Banks cannot create money without limit. They are constrained by the interest rate the central bank sets, by capital rules, by whether borrowers want loans, and by the fear of a **bank run**: if everyone asks for their deposits as cash at once, no bank can pay, because the cash was never there. That is why governments insure deposits and why a queue outside a bank is the most frightening picture in finance.

visual.title: What UK money is made of (Bank of England, 2014)

spotlights.name: The Bank of England
spotlights.spot_it: A windowless fortress of stone columns on Threadneedle Street in the City of London.
spotlights.story_md: The Bank of England was created in **1694** to lend **£1.2 million** to King William III for his war with France. In return its subscribers got a charter and the right to issue notes. Over three centuries it became the government's banker, the lender of last resort and, from 1946, a state-owned central bank. Its outer wall has no ground-floor windows, a design by **Sir John Soane** meant to resist mobs. Its nickname, 'the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street', comes from a 1797 cartoon by James Gillray, drawn when the Bank stopped paying gold for its notes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The template for central banks everywhere, including the RBI.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bank born to fund a war became the model for every central bank.

spotlights.name: 'Money creation in the modern economy'
spotlights.when: Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin, 14 March 2014
spotlights.spot_it: A short, plain article with simple balance-sheet diagrams that became one of the most-read central bank papers ever.
spotlights.story_md: Three Bank of England economists, **Michael McLeay, Amar Radia and Ryland Thomas**, wrote it to correct the textbook view. Key lines: banks do not act simply as intermediaries lending out savers' deposits, and they do not 'multiply up' central bank reserves. Lending creates deposits. The companion article noted that **97%** of the money the UK public holds is bank deposits; only 3% is notes and coins. Heterodox economists had argued this for decades, and seeing a central bank say it outright made the paper famous. The Bank also released a short video explaining it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It settled, from the top, how modern money is made.
spotlights.memory_hook: Your bank did not lend you someone's savings; it typed your loan into being.

spotlights.name: The run on Northern Rock
spotlights.spot_it: Long queues of worried savers outside a high-street bank branch, a scene Britain had not seen in generations.
spotlights.story_md: Northern Rock, a fast-growing mortgage lender from Newcastle, funded itself by borrowing in wholesale markets. When those markets froze in August 2007, it asked the Bank of England for emergency help. News leaked on **13 September**, and the next morning savers queued outside branches to pull their money out. It was the first run on a British bank in about **140 years**, since Overend, Gurney and Co. in 1866. About **£1 billion** left in a day. The government guaranteed all deposits and nationalised the bank in **February 2008**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows how deposits, which feel like cash, are really a promise.
spotlights.memory_hook: Britain's first bank run in 140 years started with a news leak.

spotlights.name: Ireland's six months without banks
spotlights.spot_it: Pub counters and shop tills piled with handwritten cheques, during a bank strike that shut every major Irish bank.
spotlights.story_md: In **1970** a pay dispute closed Ireland's main banks for about **six and a half months**. You might expect the economy to freeze. It did not. People kept writing cheques to each other, even though no bank could clear them. Shops and, by most accounts, **pubs** cashed cheques for customers they knew, and those cheques passed from hand to hand like private money. Economist **Antoin Murphy** later argued that a small, close-knit society used personal knowledge as a credit check. When banks reopened, the backlog took until early 1971 to clear. The economy had grown regardless.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that money is credit plus trust; the trust can come from a publican.
spotlights.memory_hook: For six months, Irish pubs were the banks.

sections.title: Sticks, taxes and the state
sections.intro_md:
If money is credit, why do we use the state's credit and not, say, Tata's or a local pub's? One influential answer is that the state demands **taxes**, and it chooses what it will accept in payment. Whatever the state accepts, everyone needs.

This is the **state theory of money**, set out by the German economist **Georg Friedrich Knapp** in **1905** and later called **chartalism**. In **1913** the British diplomat **Alfred Mitchell-Innes** pushed it further, arguing that a coin or note is simply a record of a debt, and that a buyer pays by handing over a credit he holds on someone else. Keynes reviewed Mitchell-Innes's work warmly.

The strongest evidence comes from England, where for more than 600 years the government's accounts were kept on notched hazel sticks, and from Nazi Germany, where the most ambitious forgery operation in history tried to destroy Britain's money by destroying trust in it.

spotlights.name: Exchequer tally sticks
spotlights.spot_it: A long, flat stick of hazel with notches of different widths cut along one edge and writing in ink on the side.
spotlights.story_md: England's Exchequer recorded payments by cutting notches in a stick: a notch the width of a palm for £1,000, a thumb for £100, a little finger for £20, and so on. The stick was then split lengthwise. The lender kept the longer half, the **stock** (hence 'stockholder'), and the Exchequer kept the shorter **foil**. Only the two halves fitted together, so tallies were very hard to forge. Tallies could be passed to third parties and used to pay taxes, so they circulated as money. The system was abolished in **1826**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Government debt circulating as money, 600 years before modern bonds.
spotlights.memory_hook: The word 'stockholder' comes from half a split stick.

spotlights.name: The tallies that burned down Parliament
spotlights.spot_it: J. M. W. Turner's painting of an orange inferno lighting up the Thames at night, with crowds on the bank.
spotlights.story_md: After the tally system ended, cartloads of old sticks were stored at Westminster. In **October 1834** officials ordered them burned in the furnaces under the House of Lords. The workmen stuffed the furnaces all day. By evening the chimney flues had overheated and the panelling caught fire. Most of the medieval **Palace of Westminster** burned down that night, leaving Westminster Hall standing. **J. M. W. Turner** watched from the river and painted it twice. Charles Dickens later mocked the episode as the result of clinging to notched sticks for centuries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Money records so durable they destroyed the building that issued them.
spotlights.memory_hook: Old money set Parliament on fire, and Turner painted it.

spotlights.name: Operation Bernhard: forging a nation's money
spotlights.spot_it: Near-perfect white British £5 to £50 notes, printed in a Nazi concentration camp.
spotlights.story_md: Nazi Germany planned to wreck Britain's economy by flooding it with fake pounds. From **1942**, about **142 Jewish prisoners** at **Sachsenhausen** concentration camp were forced to forge Bank of England notes, cracking the paper, watermarks and serial number system. They produced notes with a face value of about **£134 million**. The air drop never happened, but the SS used the notes to pay agents and buy goods. In 1945 crates were dumped in Austria's **Lake Toplitz**; divers recovered some in 1959. The Bank of England had already stopped issuing notes above £5 in 1943, and did not bring back a larger note until the £10 of 1964.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Attacking a currency means attacking trust, not paper.
spotlights.memory_hook: Prisoners forged £134 million to save their own lives.

sections.title: Gold: the anchor and its cutting
sections.intro_md:
For most of the last 300 years, people believed that real money meant gold, and that paper was only real if you could swap it for gold. That belief has deep roots and is mostly a recent arrival.

Britain slid onto a **gold standard** by accident in **1717** and made it law in **1821**. By the 1870s most major economies had joined: a pound, a dollar or a mark meant a fixed weight of gold. It gave long-run price stability and trust across borders. It also meant that in a crisis, governments could not create money to rescue banks or jobs, which helped turn the 1929 crash into the Great Depression. Countries that left gold earliest, like Britain in 1931, recovered earliest.

After the Second World War, the **Bretton Woods** system tied other currencies to the dollar and the dollar to gold at **$35 an ounce**. On **15 August 1971**, Richard Nixon cut that last link. Since then every major currency has been **fiat money**, money by decree, backed by the state and the economy behind it rather than by metal.

rows.Fiat money: Whatever it buys; set by policy and trust
Central bank rates and bank lending

rows.Gold standard: Low on average, with sharp swings
Hard: cannot create money to stop panics
rows.Fiat money: Central bank can lend without limit

spotlights.name: Isaac Newton, Master of the Mint
spotlights.spot_it: The famous long-haired portrait by Kneller, of the physicist who spent his last 30 years running the Royal Mint.
spotlights.story_md: Newton took the job at the Royal Mint in **1696** expecting a sinecure and threw himself into it. He oversaw the recoinage of clipped silver, and he personally hunted counterfeiters, going undercover in taverns and sending at least one, **William Chaloner**, to the gallows in 1699. In **1717** he set the value of the gold guinea at **21 shillings**. That rate overvalued gold relative to silver compared with the rest of Europe, so silver flowed out of Britain and gold flowed in. Without anyone deciding it, Britain had moved onto a de facto gold standard.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The gold standard began as a rounding decision by a physicist.
spotlights.memory_hook: Newton's 21 shillings quietly put Britain on gold.

spotlights.name: Mansa Musa's gold flood
spotlights.spot_it: A crowned king on a throne holding a gold nugget, painted on the 1375 Catalan Atlas.
spotlights.story_md: Mansa Musa, ruler of the **Mali Empire**, travelled to Mecca in **1324** with a huge caravan carrying gold. In **Cairo** he and his followers spent and gave away so much that, according to the Arab historian **al-Umari**, the value of gold in Egypt fell and had not recovered twelve years later. Musa reportedly tried to fix it on the way home by borrowing gold at high interest. A European mapmaker put him on the 1375 Catalan Atlas holding a gold nugget. The episode is an early, vivid case of inflation caused by a sudden increase in the money metal.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Even gold loses value when too much of it arrives at once.
spotlights.memory_hook: One king's shopping trip crashed the price of gold in Cairo.

spotlights.name: The Bretton Woods conference

where.label: Mount Washington Hotel, Bretton Woods, New Hampshire

spotlights.spot_it: A grand white hotel with red roofs under the mountains of New Hampshire, and a small wood-panelled 'Gold Room'.
spotlights.story_md: With the war still raging, **730 delegates** from **44 Allied nations** met at the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire. They designed a new money system: currencies fixed to the US dollar, the dollar convertible to gold at **$35 an ounce** for foreign governments, and two new institutions, the **IMF** and the **World Bank**. India sent a delegation led by **R. K. Shanmukham Chetty**, with **C. D. Deshmukh**, the first Indian governor of the RBI, among its members. India argued, without much success, for the release of its sterling balances owed by Britain.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It set the rules of world money for 27 years, and created the IMF and World Bank.
spotlights.memory_hook: Forty-four nations rebuilt world money in a ski hotel.

spotlights.name: The Nixon shock
spotlights.spot_it: Official 1971 portrait of the 37th US president, taken weeks before he cut the dollar loose from gold.
spotlights.story_md: By 1971, the United States had issued far more dollars than it held gold at $35 an ounce, and foreign governments were lining up to swap dollars for bullion. After a secret weekend meeting at Camp David, **Richard Nixon** went on television on Sunday **15 August 1971** and announced that the US would 'suspend temporarily' the dollar's convertibility into gold. It was never restored. Within two years, major currencies were floating freely against each other. Nixon chose a Sunday to beat the Monday markets.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The day the world's money became fully fiat.
spotlights.memory_hook: A 'temporary' suspension in 1971 is still in force.

spotlights.name: Fort Knox Bullion Depository
spotlights.spot_it: A squat granite-and-concrete box with a single tower, behind fences on a US Army base in Kentucky.
spotlights.story_md: Built in **1936** and filled from **1937**, the depository holds about **147 million troy ounces** of gold, roughly **4,580 tonnes**, around half of the US government's gold. The vault door alone weighs over 20 tonnes, and no single person knows the full combination. Here is the oddity: on the government's books, all US gold is still valued at the old statutory price of **$42.22 an ounce**, set in 1973. Gold traded above **$5,000** an ounce in early 2026. Since 1971, none of it backs a single dollar.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Gold remains a reserve asset even though it no longer backs money.
spotlights.memory_hook: America values its gold at $42.22 an ounce on paper.

sections.title: When money breaks
sections.intro_md:
Fiat money's great danger is that the issuer can print it. Usually, central banks keep inflation to a few per cent a year. But when a government cannot pay its bills any other way, because of war, lost territory, a collapsed tax base or plain recklessness, it can turn to the printing press. Prices rise, people spend money as fast as they can, prices rise faster, and the currency dies.

Economists call it **hyperinflation** when monthly inflation passes **50%**. The economists **Steve Hanke and Nicholas Krus** counted 56 episodes in history. Most happened in the 20th century, after paper money and before modern central bank independence.

The common thread is not the printing itself but the loss of trust. Once people expect money to be worth less tomorrow, they refuse to hold it. Each of the three cases below ended the same way: a new currency, with new rules and someone credible promising to stick to them.

visual.title: How fast prices doubled at the peak (hours)

spotlights.name: Germany, 1923
spotlights.spot_it: Banknotes overprinted with ever-larger numbers; families using piles of paper marks as wallpaper or fuel.
spotlights.story_md: To pay for the First World War and then reparations, Germany printed. After France occupied the Ruhr in **January 1923** and the government paid striking workers with new money, prices went vertical. By **November 1923** one US dollar cost about **4.2 trillion marks**. Prices doubled roughly every **3.7 days**. Workers were paid twice a day and ran to the shops before prices changed. A 1,000-mark note from 1922 was overstamped to read **one billion marks**. The crisis ended with a new currency, the **Rentenmark**, on **15 November 1923**, and a strict cap on how many were issued.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It wiped out the German middle class's savings and left a political scar.
spotlights.memory_hook: In 1923 a billion marks was a rubber stamp on a thousand.

spotlights.name: Hungary, 1946: the worst inflation ever recorded
spotlights.spot_it: Notes with long rows of zeros; the largest issued was 100 quintillion pengő, and a sextillion note was printed but never used.
spotlights.story_md: After the Second World War, Hungary's economy was shattered and Soviet reparations drained what was left. The government printed pengő to pay for everything. In **July 1946**, monthly inflation reached about **41.9 quadrillion per cent** (4.19 × 10¹⁶%), the highest rate on record. Prices doubled roughly every **15 hours**. The central bank issued a note for **100 quintillion** (10²⁰) pengő, the highest denomination ever circulated. On **1 August 1946** the forint replaced it at a rate of one forint to 400 octillion pengő. All Hungarian money in circulation that day was worth a fraction of one US cent.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The extreme limit of what loss of trust in money looks like.
spotlights.memory_hook: In 1946 Hungarian prices doubled between breakfast and the next dinner.

spotlights.name: Zimbabwe's 100 trillion dollar note
spotlights.spot_it: A blue-green note with Victoria Falls and the number 100,000,000,000,000 in large print.
spotlights.story_md: Zimbabwe's crisis followed land seizures that collapsed farm output, followed by money printing to cover the deficit. By **November 2008**, monthly inflation was estimated at **79.6 billion per cent**; prices doubled about every **24.7 hours**. The central bank issued a **Z$100 trillion** note in **January 2009**, which soon bought a few loaves of bread. Months later, the country simply abandoned its currency and used US dollars and South African rand. The notes are now sold online as souvenirs, often for more than they were worth at issue. Zimbabwe launched another new currency, the **ZiG**, in **April 2024**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most recent hyperinflation most adults remember.
spotlights.memory_hook: Zimbabwe's 100 trillion note is worth more as a souvenir.

sections.title: India's money: cowries to UPI
sections.intro_md:
India has used almost every form of money in this story, often at the same time. Cowries for the smallest purchases, silver for the big ones, hundis between cities, gold in every home, and now the world's busiest instant payment system.

The modern rupee begins with a short-lived Afghan ruler, **Sher Shah Suri**, in the 1540s. The British kept his silver standard. Independent India's rupee was managed by the RBI from 1949, and much of its recent history is about two forces pulling in opposite directions: a deep cultural trust in **cash and gold**, and a fast state-led push into **digital payments**.

That tension came to a head on **8 November 2016**, when the government withdrew 86% of the cash in circulation in one evening. It set the stage for UPI's explosion, and yet, ten years on, India has more cash circulating than ever. The rupee story is a live test of every idea in this day: trust, state power, credit, and habit.

spotlights.name: Cowries in Bengal and Odisha
spotlights.spot_it: Small white shells counted in heaps at village markets, 80 to a 'pan'.
spotlights.story_md: In eastern India, cowries imported from the Maldives remained real money for everyday purchases until the 1800s. In Bengal and Odisha they were counted in fixed units: 4 cowries made a **ganda**, 20 gandas a **pan**, and several thousand made a rupee. Rates shifted with supply, so the shell rupee could be worth 2,500 or 5,000 cowries depending on the decade. In **Sylhet**, the East India Company collected land revenue in cowries late into the 18th century and had to ship them to Dhaka. The language kept the memory: 'kaudi-kaudi ko mohtaaj' means destitute.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India ran a two-tier money system for centuries: shells for the poor, silver for the rich.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bengal's small change came from Maldivian lagoons.

spotlights.name: Sher Shah Suri's rupiya
spotlights.spot_it: A thick round silver coin with Persian and Devanagari script, the ruler's name and the Islamic creed.
spotlights.story_md: **Sher Shah Suri** briefly drove the Mughal emperor Humayun out of India and, in five years of rule, reorganised the Grand Trunk Road, the land revenue and the coinage. His silver **rupiya** weighed about **178 grains**, roughly **11.5 grams**, and carried his name in Devanagari as well as Persian. The word comes from Sanskrit **rūpya**, meaning wrought or stamped silver. The Mughals kept his standard, the East India Company kept the Mughals', and the name spread to Pakistan, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Mauritius and Indonesia's rupiah.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The direct ancestor of the coin and note in your pocket.
spotlights.memory_hook: A five-year reign gave South Asia a 480-year-old word.

spotlights.name: The ₹ symbol
spotlights.spot_it: A Devanagari 'ra' with a horizontal bar on top and a second line through it.
spotlights.story_md: Until 2010 the rupee had no symbol of its own; people wrote Rs. The government ran an open competition and chose the design of **D. Udaya Kumar**, then a postgraduate at IIT Bombay, from thousands of entries. The Union Cabinet approved it on **15 July 2010**. It blends the Devanagari letter **र (ra)** with the Roman capital **R**, with two horizontal lines that suggest both the tricolour and an equals sign for balance. It reached coins in 2011 and Unicode the same year. Udaya Kumar went on to teach design at IIT Guwahati.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A currency's symbol is a statement of national confidence.
spotlights.memory_hook: ₹ is a ra and an R holding up a flag.

spotlights.name: Demonetisation
spotlights.spot_it: Long lines of people outside ATMs and banks across India in November and December 2016.
spotlights.story_md: In a televised address, Prime Minister **Narendra Modi** announced that **₹500 and ₹1,000** notes would cease to be legal tender at midnight. Those notes made up about **86%** of the value of cash in circulation, around **₹15.41 lakh crore**. The aims were to flush out black money and counterfeit notes and push digital payments. People queued for weeks to exchange or deposit old notes. By the RBI's count in August 2018, about **₹15.31 lakh crore**, or **99.3%**, had come back into banks. Economists still debate its costs and benefits.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The largest sudden currency withdrawal in modern history, and a test of trust in cash.
spotlights.memory_hook: In one evening, 86% of India's cash stopped being money.

spotlights.name: UPI: the world's busiest real-time payments system
spotlights.spot_it: A printed QR code taped to a vegetable cart or a tea stall counter, and a phone beeping 'payment received'.
spotlights.story_md: The **Unified Payments Interface**, built by the **National Payments Corporation of India**, let any bank account pay any other instantly using a phone and a simple address. Free to users and open to every bank and app, it grew slowly until demonetisation pushed millions to try it. In **August 2026** it handled a record **24.51 billion** transactions worth about **₹29.8 lakh crore**. In September 2026 average daily transactions passed **800 million** for the first time. Two apps, PhonePe and Google Pay, carry close to four in five UPI payments.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made digital money normal for street vendors before many rich countries.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eight hundred million payments a day, many smaller than a cup of chai.

spotlights.name: Gold in Indian homes
spotlights.when: Ongoing; peaks at Dhanteras and Akshaya Tritiya
spotlights.spot_it: Bridal sets, bangles and coins bought at festival time and kept in steel cupboards or bank lockers.
spotlights.story_md: Indian households are estimated to hold about **25,000 tonnes** of gold, more than the official reserves of the top ten central banks combined; estimates range higher when temple gold is included. For many families, especially in villages, gold is savings, insurance and a woman's own property (**stridhan**) all at once. It can be pawned for a loan within an hour. Buying spikes on **Dhanteras** and **Akshaya Tritiya**. The RBI itself holds **880.52 tonnes**. Gold's share in India's foreign reserves rose to about **17%** in 2026 as prices hit records.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Gold remains India's most trusted store of value outside the banking system.
spotlights.memory_hook: India's real gold reserve is in its kitchen cupboards.

spotlights.name: The e-rupee
spotlights.spot_it: A wallet app showing digital ₹ 'notes' in denominations, issued directly by the RBI.
spotlights.story_md: The **e₹** is a central bank digital currency: a direct claim on the RBI, held in a digital wallet, rather than a deposit at a commercial bank. The RBI launched a wholesale pilot on **1 November 2022** and a retail pilot on **1 December 2022**. Adoption has been slow because UPI already works so well: in **February 2026**, about **₹689 crore** of e-rupee was in circulation, against more than **₹40 lakh crore** of paper notes, less than 0.02%. The RBI has added offline payments and programmable features to find uses UPI cannot serve.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It tests whether state digital cash adds anything to a fast private system.
spotlights.memory_hook: India's digital rupee is a drop beside its paper rupee.

sections.title: Money without a bank: phones and code
sections.intro_md:
The last two decades have produced two big experiments in money outside the old banking system. One came from a mobile phone company in Kenya and quietly changed millions of lives. The other came from an anonymous programmer and became a global obsession.

**M-Pesa** proved that a telecom company could run a payment system for people banks had ignored. **Bitcoin** asked a deeper question: can money exist with no issuer at all, its scarcity enforced by mathematics and its ledger kept by thousands of strangers? Read alongside Yap, Bitcoin is oddly familiar: a public ledger that everyone checks, with tokens that never move.

Seventeen years on, Bitcoin works well as a speculative asset and poorly as everyday money: its price swings too much to be a good unit of account. The newer **stablecoins**, crypto tokens pegged to the dollar, are closer to old-fashioned bank money, and in 2025 the United States began regulating them as such.

spotlights.name: M-Pesa in Kenya
spotlights.spot_it: Green-painted kiosks with the M-PESA logo, where agents swap cash for phone credit and back.
spotlights.story_md: Safaricom launched **M-Pesa** ('pesa' is Swahili for money) in **March 2007**. Users deposit cash with a local agent and send it to anyone by text message, on basic phones. Within a few years most Kenyan adults used it. In **2016** economists **Tavneet Suri and William Jack** published a study in Science estimating that access to M-Pesa lifted about **194,000 Kenyan households**, about **2%**, out of extreme poverty, with the biggest effect among households headed by women. People could save safely and get help from relatives quickly when hit by illness or a bad harvest.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Mobile money showed that the payment layer can come before the bank account.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Kenya, money became a text message in 2007.

spotlights.name: Bitcoin
spotlights.when: White paper 31 October 2008; first block 3 January 2009
spotlights.spot_it: An orange circle with a slanted B and two vertical strokes; 'physical bitcoins' are novelty coins.
spotlights.story_md: An unknown person or group called **Satoshi Nakamoto** published a nine-page paper on **31 October 2008** describing peer-to-peer electronic cash. The first block, mined on **3 January 2009**, embedded a newspaper headline about a second bank bailout. The design caps supply at **21 million** coins, and a network of computers competes to add blocks to a public ledger. The price peaked above **$126,000** in **October 2025** and traded around **$83,000 to $85,000** in early October 2026. El Salvador made it legal tender in 2021, then made accepting it voluntary in **January 2025**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first working money with no issuer, and a test of what money needs.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bitcoin is a Yap stone made of maths.

spotlights.name: The 10,000-bitcoin pizzas
spotlights.spot_it: A Papa John's pizza outlet in Jacksonville, Florida, remembered every year on 'Bitcoin Pizza Day'.
spotlights.story_md: On **22 May 2010**, programmer **Laszlo Hanyecz** in Florida paid **10,000 bitcoin** to a stranger on a forum, who ordered him two Papa John's pizzas worth about **$41**. It is the first well-known purchase of a physical good with bitcoin. At the October 2025 peak, those coins would have been worth over **$1.2 billion**. Hanyecz says he has no regrets: someone had to show the thing could buy something. The date is now celebrated as Bitcoin Pizza Day.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A medium of exchange is only money once someone accepts it for real goods.
spotlights.memory_hook: The most expensive dinner in history cost $41 at the time.

sections.title: Myths about money, checked
sections.intro_md:
Money is surrounded by confident beliefs that do not survive contact with evidence. Here are the most common, with what the record says.

**'Money started with barter.'** No barter economy has been found. Credit and accounts came first.

**'My money is backed by gold.'** Not since 1971 for the dollar, and not for the rupee either. The RBI holds gold as a reserve asset, not as a promise to swap notes.

**'Banks lend out savers' deposits.'** Mostly they create new deposits when they lend, as the Bank of England put it in 2014.

**'Printing money always causes inflation.'** Usually, when it outruns output. But Japan, the US and Europe expanded central bank money hugely after 2008 with low inflation for a decade. It depends on whether the money is spent and whether the economy can produce more.

**'Cash is dying.'** In payments, its share is falling. In stock, it keeps growing: India's notes in circulation and the number of US $100 bills both hit records in the 2020s.

**'Roman soldiers were paid in salt.'** No good evidence.

Banks create most money when they lend

data.evidence: True in hyperinflations; weak link after 2008
Payments share falls; stock of notes rises
Only a stray remark by Pliny

spotlights.name: The first cash machine, and why cash refuses to die
spotlights.spot_it: A gold-painted cash machine and a blue plaque on a Barclays branch in Enfield, north London.
spotlights.story_md: The world's first cash dispenser opened at **Barclays in Enfield** on **27 June 1967**, invented by a team led by **John Shepherd-Barron**. There were no plastic cards yet: customers used paper vouchers marked with a mildly radioactive carbon-14 compound. The first withdrawal was made by the comedy actor **Reg Varney**. Sixty years later, cash use at tills is falling in most countries, yet the stock of cash keeps rising. At the end of **2024** there were **19.2 billion** US $100 notes in circulation, more than $1 notes, and Federal Reserve research suggests most are held abroad or as savings.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Cash survives as a store of value and an emergency backup, not just for shopping.
spotlights.memory_hook: There are more US $100 bills than $1 bills.

spotlights.name: Does printing money cause inflation?
spotlights.spot_it: A heavy iron coin press, the old picture of 'printing money'.
spotlights.story_md: The **quantity theory** says that if the amount of money grows faster than the goods it buys, prices rise. History supports it in extremes: every hyperinflation above was fuelled by printing. But the link is loose in normal times. After **2008**, central banks in the US, UK, Europe and Japan created trillions in new reserves through quantitative easing, and inflation stayed low for over a decade, because banks held the reserves rather than lending them out. Then in **2021 to 2022**, pandemic spending plus supply shocks did push inflation to 40-year highs in many countries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The honest answer is 'it depends on whether the new money gets spent'.
spotlights.memory_hook: Money printing is a fire that needs spending as fuel.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
Money is changing faster in this decade than at any time since 1971. Here is where things stand in late 2026.

**Coins are being retired.** The United States struck its last circulating penny on **12 November 2025**, because each one cost nearly four cents to make. **Gold has been on a wild ride**: the LBMA price set a record of about **$5,500** an ounce on **29 January 2026**, then fell back to around $4,000 to $4,200 by June. Central banks, including the RBI, were big buyers through 2025, a sign of reduced trust in holding only dollars.

**Stablecoins are going mainstream.** The US **GENIUS Act**, signed on **18 July 2025**, created the first federal rules for dollar-backed tokens; the total market was around **$300 billion** in 2026, but final regulations were still unfinished by September 2026. **Europe is building a digital euro**, with the ECB aiming for legislation by the end of 2026, a pilot from 2027 and possible first issuance in **2029**. And in India, UPI kept setting records, passing **800 million** payments a day in September 2026.

spotlights.name: The end of the US penny
spotlights.spot_it: A small copper-coloured coin with Abraham Lincoln's profile, first issued with his face in 1909.
spotlights.story_md: On **12 November 2025**, at the Philadelphia Mint, Treasury Secretary **Scott Bessent** and Treasurer **Brandon Beach** watched the press strike the last circulating one-cent coin, ending more than **230 years** of production. Each penny cost almost **3.7 cents** to make. Pennies remain legal tender, and the American Bankers Association estimated about **250 billion** still in circulation. Shops began rounding cash totals to the nearest five cents. Canada had already scrapped its penny in **2012**, and India withdrew all coins below 50 paise in **2011**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: When a coin costs more than its face value, the state stops minting it.
spotlights.memory_hook: America spent 3.7 cents to make every cent.

spotlights.name: Gold's record run
spotlights.spot_it: Stacks of stamped, brick-shaped gold bars, the 400-ounce 'good delivery' size held by central banks.
spotlights.story_md: Gold rose through **2025**, passing $4,000 an ounce in October, driven by central bank buying, fears about government debt, and doubts about US policy. On **29 January 2026** the LBMA morning price hit a record of about **$5,501.70**. Then it fell hard, by roughly a quarter, to around $4,000 by late June 2026. For Indian households, whose jewellery doubles as savings, the rally made them on paper hundreds of billions of dollars richer. The swing is a reminder that gold is a store of value over decades, not months.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Gold's comeback shows how trust in fiat money can wobble.
spotlights.memory_hook: Gold gained more in 18 months than in the previous decade, then dropped a quarter.

spotlights.name: Stablecoins and the GENIUS Act
spotlights.spot_it: Crypto tokens like USDT and USDC, each meant to stay worth exactly one US dollar.
spotlights.story_md: A stablecoin is a token on a blockchain that promises to be redeemable for one dollar, backed by cash and short-term US government bonds. Economically it looks like an old private banknote. The **GENIUS Act**, signed by President Trump on **18 July 2025**, requires full reserves, monthly disclosures and federal or state licences. By mid-2026 the market was about **$300 to $320 billion**, led by Tether's USDT at around $184 billion and Circle's USDC at around $73 billion. Regulators missed the one-year deadline for final rules; the requirements default to taking effect by **18 January 2027**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Private money is back, this time on blockchains, and governments are deciding the rules.
spotlights.memory_hook: A stablecoin is a 19th-century private banknote in a crypto wallet.

spotlights.name: The digital euro
spotlights.when: Preparation phase from October 2025; issuance aimed for 2029
spotlights.spot_it: The ECB's twin glass towers on the Main river in Frankfurt, where the digital euro is being designed.
spotlights.story_md: The **European Central Bank** wants a digital euro so Europeans can pay with central bank money online, not only with US card networks and big tech wallets. In **October 2025** the ECB moved the project into a new phase, aiming for a pilot from **mid-2027** and first issuance in **2029**, if EU lawmakers pass the regulation in 2026. In **April 2026** ECB board member **Piero Cipollone** urged the EU to finish the law by year-end. Critics worry about privacy and bank deposits draining away; the draft caps how much each person can hold.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the largest test yet of state digital cash in a rich economy.
spotlights.memory_hook: Europe is building a digital note so its money is not run by card companies.

sections.title: What money actually is: the recap
sections.intro_md:
Put the evidence together and a clear picture emerges.

**Money is a social technology for keeping score.** It records who owes what to whom, in a unit everyone recognises. The token, a rai stone, a cowrie, a coin, a ₹500 note or a UPI entry, is just the way the score is kept.

**Credit came first.** Mesopotamian accounts in barley and silver predate coins by 2,500 years. The barter story is a thought experiment, not history.

**Coins and paper added guarantees.** A stamp on metal, then a promise on paper, let strangers trust each other. Each time, issuers were tempted to over-issue, from Rome's denarius to the Ming note to Weimar's marks.

**Most modern money is bank credit.** About 97% of UK money is deposits created by lending. Central banks steer it with interest rates and stand behind it in crises.

**The anchor is trust, not metal.** Since 1971 no major currency has been backed by gold. What keeps a rupee worth something is the RBI, the tax system, and an economy that produces things people want.

**The future is a contest between public and private digital money:** UPI and the e-rupee, stablecoins, digital euros. The question underneath has not changed since Yap: whose record do we trust?

cards.back: No barter economy has ever been documented; communities ran on credit and obligations first (Humphrey, 1985).

best_facts.fact: On Yap, a family was counted rich because of a giant stone that had sunk to the seabed generations earlier. Nobody had seen it, but everyone agreed it was theirs.
best_facts.why_surprising: Wealth that no living person had ever seen.

best_facts.fact: About 97% of the money people hold in the UK is bank deposits, and most of it was created by banks typing new loans into accounts.
best_facts.why_surprising: Most money is not printed by the state at all.

best_facts.fact: In 1834 officials burned centuries of old wooden tally sticks in the furnaces under the House of Lords, and the fire destroyed most of the Palace of Westminster.
In July 1946 Hungarian prices doubled about every 15 hours, and the government printed a 100 quintillion pengő note.
best_facts.why_surprising: Prices doubled between breakfast and the next dinner.

best_facts.fact: During a 1970 bank strike, Ireland went about six and a half months without its main banks, and the economy kept running on cheques passed hand to hand.
best_facts.why_surprising: A modern economy survived half a year with no banks.

best_facts.fact: No anthropologist has ever documented an economy that ran on barter. Credit and accounts came first.
best_facts.why_surprising: The textbook origin story of money has no evidence.

best_facts.fact: The US government still values its gold at $42.22 an ounce on its books, while the market price passed $5,000 in early 2026.
best_facts.why_surprising: An official price more than 100 times too low.

best_facts.fact: On 22 May 2010 a programmer paid 10,000 bitcoin for two pizzas worth about $41. At the 2025 peak those coins were worth over $1.2 billion.
best_facts.why_surprising: The most expensive takeaway in history.

best_facts.fact: Sweden's 17th-century copper plate money could weigh nearly 20 kg per piece, which is why Europe's first banknotes were printed there in 1661.
best_facts.why_surprising: Paper money was invented to save backs.

best_facts.fact: After demonetisation in 2016, about 99.3% of the cancelled ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes came back to the banks.
best_facts.why_surprising: Almost none of the 'black money' was destroyed.

best_facts.fact: Isaac Newton spent 30 years running the Royal Mint, hunted counterfeiters in disguise, and accidentally put Britain on the gold standard in 1717.
best_facts.why_surprising: The physicist who invented the gold standard by rounding.

best_facts.fact: The Chinese character for valuables, 貝, began as a picture of a cowrie shell, and it still appears inside the characters for buy and sell.
best_facts.why_surprising: A shell is written into the Chinese word for money.

best_facts.fact: Mansa Musa of Mali spent so much gold in Cairo in 1324 that the value of gold there was still depressed twelve years later.
There are more US $100 notes in circulation than $1 notes: about 19.2 billion at the end of 2024.
best_facts.why_surprising: Cash is growing as a store of value even as card use rises.

best_facts.fact: The ₹1 note is issued by the Government of India and signed by the finance secretary; every other rupee note is issued by the RBI.
best_facts.why_surprising: Your smallest note has a different issuer.

best_facts.fact: UPI passed 800 million transactions a day on average in September 2026, after a record 24.51 billion in August.
best_facts.why_surprising: More than half a payment per Indian per day.

best_facts.fact: Each US penny cost about 3.7 cents to make before production ended on 12 November 2025.
best_facts.why_surprising: The coin was worth a quarter of its cost.

side_dish.title: The pain of paying: why UPI makes spending easy
side_dish.body_md:
Hand over a ₹500 note and you feel a small sting. Tap a phone and the sting nearly vanishes. Behavioural economists call this the **pain of paying**, and it changes how much people spend.

The best-known test came in **2001**. Drazen Prelec and Duncan Simester at **MIT** ran sealed-bid auctions for sold-out Boston Celtics tickets. Half the students were told they would have to pay in cash, half by credit card. The card group bid far more, in one auction around **twice as much**. Same tickets, same students, different feeling of money leaving.

Brain-imaging studies by Brian Knutson, Prelec and colleagues found that high prices activate the **insula**, a region linked to discomfort, and that this predicts when people refuse to buy. Anything that blurs the moment of payment, such as cards, saved wallets, one-click checkout or UPI autopay, dulls that signal.

The link to today's topic is direct. If money is a record, not a thing, then the record can be made almost invisible. Cash makes the record physical: you watch the pile shrink. Digital money keeps the record in a database you rarely look at.

A practical takeaway: if you want to spend less, add friction back. Check your UPI history weekly, set a monthly cap in your app, or use cash for one category, like eating out, for a month and see what happens.

offline_task.title: Read your money like a historian
offline_task.body_md:
Take one banknote and two coins from your wallet. Spend ten minutes on them.

**1. Find the promise.** On a rupee note above ₹1, find the line 'I promise to pay the bearer the sum of...' and the governor's signature. Ask: pay in what? Since there is no gold behind it, the honest answer is another note. That sentence is a fossil from the gold era.

**2. Find the trust machinery.** Hold the note to the light and find the watermark portrait, the security thread that shifts colour, the see-through register and the micro-lettering. Each one exists because, as Operation Bernhard showed, attacking money means attacking trust.

**3. Find the history.** Look for the ₹ sign (2010), the year on each coin, and the languages panel listing the denomination in 15 Indian languages. Note which languages you can read.

**4. Ask an elder.** Ask a parent or grandparent what they remember about paise coins, the first time they used an ATM, demonetisation night, or how gold was bought for a wedding. Write down one story. That is an oral source, the kind historians of money rely on.
